title: Requirements and real-time communication architecture
description: Project: Requirements and real-time communication architecture. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: A collaborative communication platform must support real-time messaging, presence, and notification delivery across web and mobile clients. The architecture you design determines whether the product feels responsive or laggy, and whether it remains stable under burst traffic. In this lesson, you will explore the requirements that drive architectural decisions and how real-time transport choices affect latency, throughput, and operational complexity.

items: Gather functional and non-functional requirements before choosing any transport or database
Distinguish between real-time guarantees: delivery, ordering, exactly-once, and at-least-once
Evaluate WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and long-polling against your actual client base and network conditions
Model expected scale: concurrent connections, messages per second, and peak burst factors
Identify failure modes early: network drops, server restarts, message broker outages
Plan for horizontal scaling from the start; stateless application servers with a shared message bus
Define SLAs and SLOs for latency, delivery, and uptime before writing any infrastructure code

terms.definition: A communication channel that delivers messages with low, predictable latency, typically WebSocket, SSE, or gRPC bidirectional streaming.
A messaging guarantee where the recipient receives a message exactly one time, even if the sender or network retries.
A guarantee that the message will be delivered one or more times; the consumer must deduplicate.
The number of simultaneous open connections the server must support, which directly affects memory, CPU, and load balancer configuration.
A periodic ping or pong message used to detect dead connections and keep NAT bindings alive.

data.text: Choosing the wrong transport or scaling model early can force a rewrite when traffic grows. A team that skips requirements gathering may build a chat app with WebSocket and discover later that mobile carriers drop idle connections after sixty seconds, breaking presence. Taking the time to understand scale, reliability, and client diversity prevents expensive pivots.

data.title: Measure scale before designing
data.text: Do not assume that your architecture must support millions of concurrent users on day one. Start with a realistic estimate: one hundred concurrent users, one message per second per user, and a peak burst factor of three during broadcast events. Design for that target, then document the scaling path when you hit eighty percent of capacity.

cards.title: WebSocket
cards.description: Full-duplex TCP connection over HTTP upgrade.
cons: Load balancer sticky sessions or pub/sub needed

cards.title: Long-polling
cards.description: Client issues request; server holds it open until data is available.

items: At-most-once: fire and forget. Use for non-critical telemetry or ephemeral typing indicators.
At-least-once: persist before acknowledge. Use for chat messages where loss is unacceptable; the consumer must deduplicate.
Exactly-once: combine persistence, idempotency keys, and deduplication windows. Use for financial notifications or compliance-critical alerts.

data.title: Write a requirements document
data.description: Draft a one-page requirements document for a collaborative communication platform. Include functional requirements, non-functional requirements, and explicit scale targets.
steps: List five functional requirements: send message, receive message, typing indicator, online presence, notification delivery.

List five non-functional requirements: p99 latency under two hundred milliseconds, ninety-nine point nine percent uptime, support for ten thousand concurrent WebSocket connections, message retention for thirty days, end-to-end encryption optionality.
Write scale estimates: daily active users, messages per second, peak burst multiplier, and storage growth per month.
Identify three failure modes and describe the user-visible impact of each.
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a document that makes transport and database choices obvious because the requirements leave little ambiguity.

data.title: Summary
points: Requirements drive architecture; do not skip this step
Choose transport based on client diversity, not trend
Plan for exactly-once or at-least-once semantics explicitly
Document scale targets and failure modes before coding
data.takeaway: A solid requirements phase prevents architectural rewrites later and makes every downstream decision easier to justify.
